Mini-Task 8 — Yes/No Spoken-Word Classification¶

Digital Speech Processing · A complete, reproducible worked solution¶

Dataset: YesNo (OpenSLR SLR1, the same data as torchaudio.datasets.YESNO) · Features: MFCC + Δ implemented from scratch in NumPy · Classifiers: SVM, Neural Network (MLP), k-NN, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gaussian Naïve Bayes

Contents

  1. Introduction — objective, significance, requirements
  2. Environment and reproducibility
  3. The dataset
  4. Word segmentation (energy-based VAD) — the critical step
  5. Feature extraction (MFCC pipeline, step by step)
  6. Evaluation protocol
  7. Classifiers and hyper-parameter tuning
  8. Results

  13. Check your understanding

1. Introduction¶

1.1 The problem¶

A customer-service department wants an automatic telephone operator that asks questions which can be answered with a single word, yes or no, and then decides which of the two words the caller said. Everything the system knows about the caller is the audio signal of the answer, so the task is a speech classification problem: map a short waveform $x[n]$ to a label $y \in \{\text{NO}, \text{YES}\}$.

1.2 Objective of the exercise¶

Train and compare at least four classifiers (including an SVM and a neural network) that recognise whether a spoken word is “yes” or “no” on the YesNo dataset, and judge them with a sound evaluation protocol.

In this notebook we go beyond the minimum and cover the whole chain:

Stage What we do
Data Load 60 recordings, read the label sequence from each file name
Segmentation Cut every recording into its 8 individual words with an energy-based voice activity detector
Features Build MFCC and Δ-MFCC by hand and summarise each word as a 52-dimensional vector
Models Tune and compare six classifiers
Evaluation Speaker/recording-aware hold-out test, nested grouped cross-validation, confusion matrices, ROC, confidence intervals
Experiments Feature ablation, effect of standardisation, robustness to noise, and a complete “telephone operator” demo

1.3 Why this exercise matters¶

  • It is the smallest realistic instance of keyword spotting, the technology behind voice commands (“yes”, “no”, “stop”) in phones, cars and call centres.
  • It shows the classical speech-recognition recipe: signal → short-time analysis → perceptually motivated features (MFCC) → statistical classifier. Modern deep models replace some blocks, but the same ideas (framing, spectra, Mel scale) remain at their core.
  • It teaches three habits that matter far beyond this dataset: verify your labels (a wrong segmentation silently corrupts the data), split by the right unit (by recording, not by word, to avoid leakage) and never trust a single accuracy number (report uncertainty).

2. Environment and reproducibility¶

Only standard scientific-Python packages are needed (numpy, scipy, pandas, matplotlib, scikit-learn). The MFCC front-end is written from scratch so that every step can be inspected. A fixed random seed makes every number in this notebook reproducible.

3. The dataset¶

3.1 What is in it?¶

The YesNo corpus (OpenSLR resource SLR1, created for the Kaldi project) contains 60 recordings by one male speaker speaking Hebrew. Each recording consists of 8 words, every word being either ken (“yes”) or lo (“no”), in random order. The audio is mono, 16-bit PCM, sampled at 8 kHz.

There is no separate transcript: the word sequence is encoded in the file name, with 1 = yes and 0 = no. For example

0_1_1_0_0_1_1_0.wav ⟹ NO, YES, YES, NO, NO, YES, YES, NO.

Consequence. Labels belong to the whole recording, not to individual words. Before any classifier can be trained, each recording has to be cut into its 8 words and every word has to be matched with the right label (Section 4).

3.2 Loading the data¶

The cell below looks for a folder called waves_yesno. If it is not found, it downloads the dataset (first from OpenSLR, then from a public GitHub mirror of the same 60 files). You can also point to your own copy with the environment variable YESNO_DIR.

In [3]:
def _extract_tar(data, dest):
    with tarfile.open(fileobj=io.BytesIO(data), mode="r:gz") as tf:
        for m in tf.getmembers():
            if m.isfile() and m.name.endswith(".wav"):          # extract only the wav files (no path tricks)
                (dest / Path(m.name).name).write_bytes(tf.extractfile(m).read())

def _extract_zip(data, dest):
    with zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(data)) as zf:
        for n in zf.namelist():
            if "waves_yesno/" in n and n.endswith(".wav"):
                (dest / Path(n).name).write_bytes(zf.read(n))

SOURCES = [("OpenSLR (US mirror)", "https://us.openslr.org/resources/1/waves_yesno.tar.gz", _extract_tar),
           ("OpenSLR (EU mirror)", "https://openslr.elda.org/resources/1/waves_yesno.tar.gz", _extract_tar),
           ("GitHub mirror",       "https://github.com/keighrim/kaldi-yesno-tutorial/archive/refs/heads/master.zip", _extract_zip)]

def locate_dataset(dest="data/waves_yesno"):
    candidates = [os.environ.get("YESNO_DIR"), "waves_yesno", "data/waves_yesno", "/content/waves_yesno",
                  "/content/data/waves_yesno", str(Path.home() / "data" / "waves_yesno")]
    for c in candidates:
        if c and Path(c).is_dir() and len(list(Path(c).glob("*.wav"))) == 60:
            print(f"Found local dataset: {Path(c).resolve()}")
            return Path(c)
    dest = Path(dest); dest.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for name, url, extractor in SOURCES:
        try:
            print(f"Downloading from {name} ...")
            data = urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=30).read()
            extractor(data, dest)
            if len(list(dest.glob("*.wav"))) == 60:
                print(f"  OK -> {dest.resolve()}")
                return dest
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"  not available ({type(e).__name__}); trying the next source")
    raise FileNotFoundError("Could not obtain the YesNo dataset. Download waves_yesno.tar.gz from "
                            "https://www.openslr.org/1/ , extract it, and set YESNO_DIR to the folder.")

DATA_DIR = locate_dataset()

def parse_label_sequence(path):
    seq = [int(t) for t in Path(path).stem.split("_")]
    assert len(seq) == 8 and set(seq) <= {0, 1}, f"unexpected file name: {path}"
    return seq

for f in files:

    assert x.dtype == np.int16 and x.ndim == 1, "expected mono 16-bit PCM"
    sample_rates.add(sr)
    recordings[f.stem] = (x.astype(np.float64) / 32768.0, parse_label_sequence(f))
assert sample_rates == {8000}, sample_rates

Observations.

4. Word segmentation (energy-based voice activity detection)¶

4.1 Why segmentation is necessary — and dangerous¶

Each file carries one label sequence for eight words. To train a word classifier we must (i) find the 8 words in the signal and (ii) pair the k-th detected word with the k-th label. If the detector misses a word, or counts a click as a word, every later label is shifted by one position and the training data is silently corrupted. A classifier trained on such data can still look “reasonable”, which is why we must verify the segmentation visually and with quality-control checks.

4.2 Short-time energy¶

Speech is non-stationary, but over about 20–30 ms it is approximately stationary. We therefore cut the signal into overlapping frames (25 ms long, a new frame every 10 ms → 200 samples with a hop of 80 samples at 8 kHz) and compute the log energy of each frame $m$:

$$E[m] = 10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{1}{L}\sum_{n=0}^{L-1} x^2[mH+n] + \varepsilon\right)\ \text{dB},\qquad L = 200,\ H = 80 .$$

The logarithm matches the ear’s roughly logarithmic loudness perception and turns the large amplitude differences between words into manageable differences in dB.

4.3 The algorithm (peak picking with prominence)¶

Every word appears as one “hill” in the log-energy curve, while clicks and breaths are much smaller hills. Our detector:

Step Operation Reason
1 Compute $E[m]$ and smooth it with a 5-frame moving average Remove frame-to-frame jitter
2 Ignore the first and last 100 ms Recordings end with a click artefact
3 Find local maxima at least 250 ms apart with prominence ≥ 10 dB A word is a hill that rises well above its surroundings
4 Keep the 8 most prominent peaks Every file contains exactly 8 words
5 Place boundaries at the energy minimum between neighbouring peaks Natural cut points
6 Trim each word to the frames within 20 dB of its own peak (and at least 6 dB above the noise floor) Remove silence and breath tails, even when neighbouring words run close together

Prominence measures how far a peak stands out above the higher of the valleys on either side. Real words stand out by tens of dB, spurious bumps by less, so ranking peaks by prominence needs no global threshold (the actual values are reported in Section 4.4).

In [6]:
FRAME_LEN, HOP = int(0.025 * SR), int(0.010 * SR)       # 200 samples (25 ms), 80 samples (10 ms)

def frame_signal(x, frame_len=FRAME_LEN, hop=HOP):
    """Cut x into overlapping frames -> array of shape (n_frames, frame_len)."""
    n_frames = 1 + (len(x) - frame_len) // hop
    idx = np.arange(frame_len)[None, :] + hop * np.arange(n_frames)[:, None]
    return x[idx]

def moving_average(v, k=5):
    pad = np.pad(v, (k // 2, k // 2), mode="edge")
    return np.convolve(pad, np.ones(k) / k, mode="valid")

def log_energy_db(x):
    return 10 * np.log10(np.mean(frame_signal(x) ** 2, axis=1) + 1e-10)

def segment_words(x, n_words=8, trim_frames=10, min_prominence_db=10.0, min_distance_frames=25,
                  drop_db=20.0, min_above_floor_db=6.0, min_dur_ms=100, max_dur_ms=900):
    """Return a dict with the detected word boundaries (in samples) and quality-control information."""
    e = moving_average(log_energy_db(x))
    core = slice(trim_frames, len(e) - trim_frames)
    floor = np.percentile(e[core], 10)                                   # noise-floor estimate
    pk, props = find_peaks(e[core], distance=min_distance_frames, prominence=min_prominence_db)
    pk = pk + trim_frames
    prom = props["prominences"]
    info = {"energy": e, "floor": floor, "n_bursts": len(pk), "segments": None, "ok": False,
            "reason": "", "margin_db": np.nan, "prom_kept": np.array([]), "prom_rejected": np.array([])}
    if len(pk) < n_words:
        info["reason"] = f"only {len(pk)} energy bursts found (expected {n_words})"
        return info
    order = np.argsort(prom)[::-1]
    keep = np.sort(order[:n_words])                                       # the 8 most prominent peaks, in time order
    info["prom_kept"], info["prom_rejected"] = prom[keep], prom[order[n_words:]]
    if len(pk) > n_words:
        info["margin_db"] = prom[order[n_words - 1]] - prom[order[n_words]]  # weakest word vs. strongest rejected bump
    pk_keep = pk[keep]
    valleys = [a + int(np.argmin(e[a:b + 1])) for a, b in zip(pk_keep[:-1], pk_keep[1:])]
    lo_bounds = [trim_frames] + valleys
    hi_bounds = valleys + [len(e) - trim_frames - 1]
    segs = []
    for p, lo, hi in zip(pk_keep, lo_bounds, hi_bounds):
        thr = max(e[p] - drop_db, floor + min_above_floor_db)
        s = p
        while s > lo and e[s] > thr: s -= 1
        t = p
        while t < hi and e[t] > thr: t += 1
        segs.append((s * HOP, min(t * HOP + FRAME_LEN, len(x))))
    durs = [(b - a) / SR * 1000 for a, b in segs]
    if min(durs) < min_dur_ms or max(durs) > max_dur_ms:
        info["reason"] = f"implausible word duration ({min(durs):.0f}-{max(durs):.0f} ms)"
        info["segments"] = segs
        return info
    info.update(segments=segs, ok=True, reason="OK")
    return info

seg_results = {name: segment_words(x) for name, (x, _) in recordings.items()}
print("Segmentation finished for", len(seg_results), "recordings.")

Segmentation finished for 60 recordings.

Interpretation. Most recordings contain exactly 8 clear bursts. In a few recordings an extra bump (a breath, or a double hump inside one word) is detected as a ninth burst; the prominence ranking discards it. The column margin shows how much more prominent the weakest accepted word is than the strongest rejected bump — a small margin flags a decision worth checking by eye (we do so in Figure 3 and Figure 3b). One recording contains only 7 audible bursts — two words were spoken without a pause between them — so its 8 labels cannot be aligned reliably. A responsible pipeline excludes it rather than guessing.

4.5 Visual verification¶

Numbers are not enough; we also look at the result. Each panel shows the waveform, the log-energy contour (dashed) and the detected words shaded with the label taken from the file name.

In [8]:
def plot_segmentation(ax, name, show_labels=True):
    x, labs = recordings[name]; r = seg_results[name]; t = np.arange(len(x)) / SR
    ax.plot(t, x, color="0.55", lw=0.4)
    ax.set_xlim(0, t[-1]); ax.set_ylim(-1, 1); ax.set_yticks([])
    ax2 = ax.twinx(); ax2.plot(np.arange(len(r["energy"])) * HOP / SR, r["energy"], "k--", lw=0.8); ax2.set_yticks([]); ax2.grid(False)
    ax2.spines["right"].set_visible(False)
    if r["segments"]:
        for (a, b), l in zip(r["segments"], labs):
            ax.axvspan(a / SR, b / SR, color=COL["yes" if l else "no"], alpha=0.30)
            if show_labels:
                ax.text((a + b) / 2 / SR, 0.80, CLASSES[l], ha="center", fontsize=8, color=COL["yes" if l else "no"], weight="bold")
    ax.set_title(f"{name}  [{r['reason']}]", fontsize=9, loc="left")

4.6 Building the word-level dataset¶

For every accepted recording we cut out the 8 words and attach three pieces of metadata: the recording it came from (the group used later for leak-free splitting), its position in the recording, and its label.

In [10]:
EXCLUDED = [n for n, r in seg_results.items() if not r["ok"]]
word_rows, word_signals = [], []
for name, (x, labs) in recordings.items():
    r = seg_results[name]
    if not r["ok"]:
        continue
    for k, ((a, b), l) in enumerate(zip(r["segments"], labs)):
        word_rows.append({"file": name, "pos": k, "label": l, "start": a, "end": b, "dur_ms": (b - a) / SR * 1000})
        word_signals.append(x[a:b].copy())
words = pd.DataFrame(word_rows)

5. Feature extraction: MFCC, step by step¶

5.1 Why not feed the raw waveform to a classifier?¶

A word is ~3 000 samples long, its length varies, and tiny time shifts change every sample value. We need a compact, fixed-length description that keeps what distinguishes the words (the spectral envelope of the vocal tract) and discards what does not (pitch, exact phase, loudness). Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs) (Davis & Mermelstein, 1980) are the classical answer.

5.2 The MFCC pipeline¶

# Stage Operation Parameters used here
1 Pre-emphasis $y[n]=x[n]-0.97\,x[n-1]$ — boosts high frequencies that carry weak consonant information $\alpha = 0.97$
2 Framing Overlapping frames, assumed stationary inside 25 ms (200 samples), hop 10 ms
3 Windowing Multiply by a Hamming window $w[n]=0.54-0.46\cos\frac{2\pi n}{L-1}$ to reduce spectral leakage Hamming
4 Power spectrum $P[k]=\frac{1}{N}\lvert \mathrm{FFT}_N\{y_w\}[k]\rvert^2$ $N = 256$ → 129 bins, 31.25 Hz each
5 Mel filter bank 26 triangular filters equally spaced on the Mel scale $m = 2595\log_{10}(1+f/700)$, 0–4 kHz 26 filters
6 Logarithm $\log(\text{filter-bank energy})$ — compresses dynamic range like the ear natural log
7 DCT-II Decorrelates the log energies; keeping the first coefficients keeps the smooth spectral envelope keep 13 (c0 … c12)
8 Δ (delta) Local slope of every coefficient over time (regression over ±2 frames) — captures how the sound changes 13 Δ-coefficients
9 Pooling Mean and standard deviation of the 26 coefficient tracks over all frames of the word → 52-D vector per word

The Mel scale is nearly linear below 1 kHz and logarithmic above it, so the filter bank has fine resolution at low frequencies and coarse resolution at high frequencies, mimicking human hearing.

In [11]:
PRE_EMPH, N_FFT, N_MELS, N_MFCC = 0.97, 256, 26, 13

def hz_to_mel(f): return 2595.0 * np.log10(1.0 + np.asarray(f, dtype=float) / 700.0)
def mel_to_hz(m): return 700.0 * (10.0 ** (np.asarray(m, dtype=float) / 2595.0) - 1.0)

def mel_filterbank(n_mels=N_MELS, n_fft=N_FFT, sr=SR, fmin=0.0, fmax=None):
    """Triangular filters equally spaced on the Mel scale -> matrix (n_mels, n_fft//2 + 1)."""
    fmax = sr / 2 if fmax is None else fmax
    edges = mel_to_hz(np.linspace(hz_to_mel(fmin), hz_to_mel(fmax), n_mels + 2))   # n_mels + 2 edge frequencies (Hz)
    freqs = np.linspace(0, sr / 2, n_fft // 2 + 1)
    fb = np.zeros((n_mels, len(freqs)))
    for m in range(n_mels):
        left, centre, right = edges[m:m + 3]
        fb[m] = np.maximum(0.0, np.minimum((freqs - left) / (centre - left), (right - freqs) / (right - centre)))
    return fb, edges, freqs

FB, MEL_EDGES, FREQS = mel_filterbank()
HAMMING = np.hamming(FRAME_LEN)

def preemphasis(x, a=PRE_EMPH):
    return np.append(x[0], x[1:] - a * x[:-1])

def logmel_spectrogram(x):
    """Stages 1-6: signal -> (n_frames, 26) log Mel filter-bank energies."""
    frames = frame_signal(preemphasis(x)) * HAMMING                     # (T, 200)
    power = np.abs(rfft(frames, n=N_FFT, axis=1)) ** 2 / N_FFT          # (T, 129)
    return np.log(np.maximum(power @ FB.T, 1e-10))                      # (T, 26)

def mfcc(x, n_mfcc=N_MFCC):
    """Stage 7: DCT-II (orthonormal) of the log Mel energies, keep the first n_mfcc coefficients."""
    return dct(logmel_spectrogram(x), type=2, axis=1, norm="ortho")[:, :n_mfcc]

def delta(feat, N=2):
    """Regression-based delta coefficients: d[t] = sum_n n (c[t+n]-c[t-n]) / (2 sum_n n^2)."""
    T = len(feat); pad = np.pad(feat, ((N, N), (0, 0)), mode="edge")
    num = sum(n * (pad[N + n:N + n + T] - pad[N - n:N - n + T]) for n in range(1, N + 1))
    return num / (2 * sum(n * n for n in range(1, N + 1)))

FEATURE_NAMES = [f"{stat}_{kind}{i}" for stat in ("mean", "std") for kind in ("mfcc", "d") for i in range(N_MFCC)]

def word_features(x):
    """Stages 1-9: one word waveform -> 52-D vector [mean(26), std(26)] of [MFCC(13), Δ(13)]."""
    x = x / (np.max(np.abs(x)) + 1e-12)                                 # peak-normalise: invariant to recording gain
    m = mfcc(x); F = np.hstack([m, delta(m)])                           # (T, 26)
    return np.concatenate([F.mean(axis=0), F.std(axis=0)])

5.3 Unit tests for the front-end¶

“Zero errors” starts with testing the building blocks. We check mathematical properties that must hold for a correct implementation.

In [12]:
# 1) Mel scale: conversion must be invertible
f_test = np.array([0, 100, 1000, 4000.0])
assert np.allclose(mel_to_hz(hz_to_mel(f_test)), f_test)
# 2) Filter bank: right shape, no empty filter, weights in [0, 1], exactly one filter peaks near each centre
assert FB.shape == (N_MELS, N_FFT // 2 + 1)
assert (FB.sum(axis=1) > 0).all() and FB.min() >= 0 and FB.max() <= 1 + 1e-12
# 3) The DCT-II matrix used must be orthonormal (D D^T = I) -> no information is lost before truncation
D = dct(np.eye(N_MELS), type=2, axis=0, norm="ortho"); assert np.allclose(D @ D.T, np.eye(N_MELS))
# 4) Delta of a linear ramp equals the slope (checked away from the edges)
ramp = 0.5 * np.arange(30)[:, None] * np.ones((1, 3)); assert np.allclose(delta(ramp)[3:-3], 0.5)
# 5) Framing: number of frames and content
fr = frame_signal(np.arange(1000.0)); assert fr.shape == (1 + (1000 - FRAME_LEN) // HOP, FRAME_LEN) and fr[1, 0] == HOP
# 6) A pure 1 kHz tone must put most of its energy in the Mel filters whose centre is close to 1 kHz
tone = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 1000 * np.arange(SR) / SR)
centre_hz = MEL_EDGES[1:-1]; peak_filter = int(np.argmax(logmel_spectrogram(tone).mean(axis=0)))
assert abs(centre_hz[peak_filter] - 1000) < 120, centre_hz[peak_filter]
# 7) Output of the full front-end: right size and finite for every word
X_all = np.vstack([word_features(s) for s in word_signals])
assert X_all.shape == (len(words), 52) and np.isfinite(X_all).all()
print("All front-end tests passed.  Feature matrix:", X_all.shape, "(words x features)")

All front-end tests passed.  Feature matrix: (472, 52) (words x features)

5.4 Worked example: one word through the whole pipeline¶

We follow a single “YES” word. The shapes printed first show how the data is transformed at every stage; Figure 4 shows what the signal looks like at each stage.

How to read Figure 4. Panel (a) selects one frame; (b) shows that windowing tapers the frame edges to zero; (c) is the fine, harmonic spectrum of the voice; (d) is the Mel filter bank that smooths this spectrum into 26 band energies; (e) stacks those energies over time (a log-Mel spectrogram) and (f) shows the 13 decorrelated MFCCs per frame. Pooling the columns of (f) and of its Δ over time gives the 52 numbers that describe the word.

5.5 Feature matrix for all words¶

The 52 features are named mean_mfcc0 … mean_mfcc12, mean_d0 … mean_d12, std_mfcc0 …, std_d0 … (d = Δ). Nothing is fitted in this step — features are computed word by word — so there is no information leak between future training and test sets.

5.6 Do the two classes look different?¶

Before training anything we check whether the features can separate the classes at all. Three views: the average log-Mel spectrum of each class, the mean of each cepstral coefficient, and a 2-D PCA projection (PCA is unsupervised, used here only for illustration).

In [14]:
mean_logmel = {c: np.mean([logmel_spectrogram(s / np.max(np.abs(s))).mean(axis=0) for s, l in zip(word_signals, y_all) if l == c], axis=0) for c in (0, 1)}
Z2 = PCA(n_components=2, random_state=SEED).fit(StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_all))
pcs = Z2.transform(StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_all))
mfcc_mean = X_all[:, :N_MFCC]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12.5, 8))
centre_hz = MEL_EDGES[1:-1]
for c, nm in ((0, "no"), (1, "yes")):
    ax[0, 0].plot(centre_hz, mean_logmel[c], marker="o", ms=3, color=COL[nm], label=nm.upper())
    ax[0, 1].errorbar(np.arange(N_MFCC) + (0.12 if c else -0.12), mfcc_mean[y_all == c].mean(0), yerr=mfcc_mean[y_all == c].std(0),
                      fmt="o", ms=4, capsize=2, color=COL[nm], label=nm.upper())
    ax[1, 0].scatter(pcs[y_all == c, 0], pcs[y_all == c, 1], s=14, alpha=0.7, color=COL[nm], label=nm.upper())

ax[0, 0].set(title="(a) Average log-Mel spectrum per class", xlabel="Filter centre frequency (Hz)", ylabel="log energy"); ax[0, 0].legend()
ax[0, 1].set(title="(b) Mean MFCC per coefficient (bars = ±1 std)", xlabel="Coefficient index", ylabel="value"); ax[0, 1].legend()
ax[1, 0].set(title=f"(c) PCA of the 52-D features ({100*Z2.explained_variance_ratio_.sum():.0f}% variance in 2 components)", xlabel="PC 1", ylabel="PC 2"); ax[1, 0].legend()
ax[1, 1].set(title="(d) Word duration", xlabel="Duration (ms)", ylabel="Number of words"); ax[1, 1].legend()

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

The figure confirms that the front-end works: the two classes occupy different regions of the Mel spectrum, their cepstral means differ (the large c0 values mainly encode overall level), and in the 2-D PCA projection the YES and NO words form two clearly separated clouds. The word duration overlaps heavily, so duration alone would be a poor feature. We therefore expect a high accuracy — the interesting questions are how reliably we can measure it and how robust it is.

6. Evaluation protocol¶

6.1 Split by recording, not by word¶

The 8 words of one recording share the same microphone, room, recording session and speaker state. If words of the same recording appear in both the training and the test set, the classifier can partly recognise the recording instead of the word, and the test score becomes over-optimistic (data leakage). We therefore keep all words of a recording together:

  • Hold-out test: GroupShuffleSplit → about 70 % of the recordings for training, 30 % for testing (whole recordings).
  • Cross-validation: GroupKFold (5 folds), again grouped by recording.
  • Hyper-parameters are tuned only on training data, using an inner grouped cross-validation. For the cross-validation estimate we use nested cross-validation (tuning is repeated inside every outer training fold) so that the reported score is not biased by the tuning.
  • Every model is a Pipeline(StandardScaler → classifier), so the scaler is fitted on training data only.

6.2 Metrics¶

YES is the positive class. With TP, TN, FP, FN taken from the confusion matrix:

Metric Definition Question it answers
Accuracy $\dfrac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}$ How often is the decision right?
Precision $\dfrac{TP}{TP+FP}$ Of the words called “yes”, how many really are?
Recall $\dfrac{TP}{TP+FN}$ Of all real “yes” words, how many were found?
F1 $\dfrac{2PR}{P+R}$ Balance of precision and recall
ROC-AUC area under TPR-vs-FPR curve Quality of the scores, independent of the threshold

Because one test word is worth 1/144 ≈ 0.7 % accuracy, we also report a 95 % Wilson confidence interval for the accuracy (Wilson, 1927): $\displaystyle \frac{\hat p + \frac{z^2}{2n} \pm z\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}+\frac{z^2}{4n^2}}}{1+\frac{z^2}{n}},\ z=1.96.$

In [15]:
X, y, groups = X_all, y_all, groups_all

# Hold-out split by recording (whole recordings go either to train or to test)
splitter = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.30, random_state=SEED)
train_idx, test_idx = next(splitter.split(X, y, groups))
X_tr, y_tr, g_tr = X[train_idx], y[train_idx], groups[train_idx]
X_te, y_te, g_te = X[test_idx], y[test_idx], groups[test_idx]

assert set(g_tr).isdisjoint(g_te), "leakage: a recording appears in both sets"
split_tbl = pd.DataFrame({"Recordings": [len(set(g_tr)), len(set(g_te))], "Words": [len(y_tr), len(y_te)],
                          "YES words": [int(y_tr.sum()), int(y_te.sum())], "NO words": [int((1 - y_tr).sum()), int((1 - y_te).sum())],
                          "% YES": [100 * y_tr.mean(), 100 * y_te.mean()]}, index=["Train", "Test"]).round(1)
display(Markdown("**Table 4 — Train/test split (no recording appears in both)**")); display(split_tbl)

def wilson_interval(k, n, z=1.96):
    p = k / n; denom = 1 + z ** 2 / n
    centre = (p + z ** 2 / (2 * n)) / denom
    half = z * math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z ** 2 / (4 * n ** 2)) / denom
    return max(0.0, centre - half), min(1.0, centre + half)

def get_scores(model, X_):
    """Continuous score for the positive class (for ROC / margins)."""
    return model.decision_function(X_) if hasattr(model, "decision_function") else model.predict_proba(X_)[:, 1]

7. Classifiers and hyper-parameter tuning¶

The task asks for at least four classifiers including an SVM and a neural network. We compare six models that represent different ideas about how to separate two classes:

# Model Idea Hyper-parameters searched
1 SVM (RBF kernel) Maximum-margin boundary in an implicit high-dimensional space $C \in \{0.1,1,10,100\}$, $\gamma \in \{\text{scale}, 10^{-3}, 10^{-2}\}$
2 Neural network (MLP) Layers of non-linear units trained by gradient descent (Adam) hidden layers $\{(32),(64,32)\}$, L2 penalty $\alpha \in \{10^{-4},10^{-2}\}$
3 k-Nearest Neighbours Vote of the k most similar training words $k \in \{3,5,7,11\}$, uniform / distance weights
4 Logistic regression Linear boundary, probabilistic output $C \in \{0.01,0.1,1,10\}$
5 Random forest Many decorrelated decision trees vote trees $\in \{100, 300\}$
6 Gaussian naïve Bayes Class-conditional Gaussians, independence assumption smoothing $\in \{10^{-9},10^{-6},10^{-3}\}$

Tuning rule. For each model, every parameter combination is scored by 5-fold grouped cross-validation on the training recordings only; the combination with the highest mean accuracy wins (ties go to the first combination in the grid; every grid starts with the simplest or default setting). The test set is not touched.

In [16]:
def model_zoo():
    scale = lambda: StandardScaler()
    return {
        "SVM (RBF)": (Pipeline([("scaler", scale()), ("clf", SVC(kernel="rbf", random_state=SEED))]),
                      {"clf__C": [0.1, 1, 10, 100], "clf__gamma": ["scale", 1e-3, 1e-2]}),
        "Neural Network (MLP)": (Pipeline([("scaler", scale()), ("clf", MLPClassifier(max_iter=3000, random_state=SEED))]),
                      {"clf__hidden_layer_sizes": [(32,), (64, 32)], "clf__alpha": [1e-4, 1e-2]}),
        "k-NN": (Pipeline([("scaler", scale()), ("clf", KNeighborsClassifier())]),
                      {"clf__n_neighbors": [3, 5, 7, 11], "clf__weights": ["uniform", "distance"]}),
        "Logistic Regression": (Pipeline([("scaler", scale()), ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000, random_state=SEED))]),
                      {"clf__C": [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10]}),
        "Random Forest": (Pipeline([("scaler", scale()), ("clf", RandomForestClassifier(random_state=SEED))]),
                      {"clf__n_estimators": [100, 300]}),
        "Gaussian NB": (Pipeline([("scaler", scale()), ("clf", GaussianNB())]),
                      {"clf__var_smoothing": [1e-9, 1e-6, 1e-3]}),
    }
ZOO = model_zoo()
inner_cv = lambda: GroupKFold(n_splits=5)

tuned, best_params, tune_score, fit_time, n_tied = {}, {}, {}, {}, {}
for name, (pipe, grid) in ZOO.items():
    gs = GridSearchCV(pipe, grid, cv=inner_cv(), scoring="accuracy", n_jobs=1, refit=True)
    gs.fit(X_tr, y_tr, groups=g_tr)
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); tuned[name] = model_zoo()[name][0].set_params(**gs.best_params_).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    fit_time[name] = time.perf_counter() - t0
    best_params[name], tune_score[name] = gs.best_params_, gs.best_score_
    sc_all = gs.cv_results_["mean_test_score"]; n_tied[name] = f"{int(np.isclose(sc_all, gs.best_score_).sum())} of {len(sc_all)}"

tune_tbl = pd.DataFrame({"Selected hyper-parameters": {n: ", ".join(f"{k.split('__')[1]}={v}" for k, v in p.items()) for n, p in best_params.items()},
                         "Grouped-CV accuracy on training set": {n: f"{100*s:.2f} %" for n, s in tune_score.items()},
                         "Settings tied at the best score": n_tied})
display(Markdown("**Table 5 — Hyper-parameters selected on the training set only**")); display(tune_tbl)

8. Results¶

8.1 Hold-out test set¶

Each tuned model — trained on the training recordings — predicts the unseen test recordings once.

8.2 How reliable is the comparison? Nested cross-validation¶

A single split is one experiment. To see the variability of each model, we repeat the whole procedure (tuning included) in a 5-fold grouped nested cross-validation over all 472 words. Every word is predicted exactly once by a model that never saw its recording, giving out-of-fold (OOF) predictions and scores.

In [19]:
outer = GroupKFold(n_splits=5)
oof_pred = {n: np.zeros(len(y), dtype=int) for n in ZOO}
oof_score = {n: np.zeros(len(y)) for n in ZOO}
fold_acc = {n: [] for n in ZOO}; fold_f1 = {n: [] for n in ZOO}
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for fold, (a, b) in enumerate(outer.split(X, y, groups)):
    for name, (pipe, grid) in ZOO.items():
        gs = GridSearchCV(model_zoo()[name][0], grid, cv=inner_cv(), scoring="accuracy", n_jobs=1, refit=True)
        gs.fit(X[a], y[a], groups=groups[a])
        oof_pred[name][b] = gs.predict(X[b]); oof_score[name][b] = get_scores(gs.best_estimator_, X[b])
        fold_acc[name].append(accuracy_score(y[b], oof_pred[name][b])); fold_f1[name].append(f1_score(y[b], oof_pred[name][b]))
print(f"Nested CV finished in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")

cv_tbl = pd.DataFrame({
    "CV accuracy (mean ± std over 5 folds)": {n: f"{100*np.mean(a):.2f} ± {100*np.std(a, ddof=1):.2f} %" for n, a in fold_acc.items()},
    "CV F1 (mean ± std)": {n: f"{np.mean(f):.4f} ± {np.std(f, ddof=1):.4f}" for n, f in fold_f1.items()},
    "Pooled OOF errors": {n: f"{int((oof_pred[n] != y).sum())} / {len(y)}" for n in ZOO},
    "Pooled OOF accuracy": {n: f"{100*accuracy_score(y, oof_pred[n]):.2f} %" for n in ZOO},
    "ROC-AUC (pooled OOF)": {n: f"{roc_auc_score(y, oof_score[n]):.4f}" for n in ZOO}})

Reading Figure 7. All models sit at (or within one word of) the ceiling, and the ROC curves of the models with perfect scores lie on top of each other in the upper-left corner (AUC = 1 means every YES word receives a higher score than every NO word). When everything is at the ceiling, accuracy cannot tell the models apart. The next section therefore asks questions that can discriminate: which features matter?, is standardisation needed? and what happens when the audio is noisy?

9. Practical experiments¶

9.1 What makes the classifier work? Baselines, feature ablation and scaling¶

We compare increasingly rich feature sets with three fixed, untuned classifiers (so that tuning cannot influence the comparison), using the same 5-fold recording-grouped cross-validation on all 472 words. The first rows are baselines that show what trivial strategies achieve.

In [22]:

Why we standardise anyway: the features live on different scales — the standard deviation of mean_mfcc0 across words is 2.41, the median over all 52 features is 0.20. Distance-based models (k-NN, RBF-SVM) and gradient-trained models can be dominated by large-scale features. On this easy dataset the measured effect is at most 0.21 percentage points (one word), i.e. not measurable — standardisation is a safe default, not a necessity here.

Reading Tables 8 and 9.

  • The baselines show how little a trivial strategy achieves: the majority-class rule is at about 50 %, and word duration alone is only moderately informative — the two classes overlap strongly in duration (Figure 5d).
  • Spectral features do the real work: the 13 mean MFCCs alone already reach the ceiling with all three classifiers, which confirms the PCA picture — the classes are almost linearly separable in MFCC space. Even just the two numbers derived from c0 (the energy-like coefficient) separate the words far better than chance, because the two words have different spectral balance (Figure 5a).
  • Adding standard deviations and Δ-coefficients gives no measurable gain on clean data (the single missing word of k-NN in the last row is within noise). A dataset this easy cannot show whether they help; noisy or multi-speaker data would be the place to test it (Exercise 2).
  • Standardisation had no measurable effect here either (Table 9). We keep it because it is cheap, harmless and essential on harder data.

9.2 Robustness to noise¶

A telephone line is never silent. We test robustness by adding white Gaussian noise to the (already segmented) test words at a controlled signal-to-noise ratio $$\mathrm{SNR_{dB}} = 10\log_{10}\frac{P_\text{signal}}{P_\text{noise}} ,$$ with SNR = 30, 20, 10, 5, 0 and −5 dB (0 dB means noise and speech have equal power). Two training conditions are compared:

  • Clean-trained: the tuned models of Section 7, trained on clean words only.
  • Noise-augmented: the same hyper-parameters, but the training set additionally contains noisy copies of every training word (SNR 20, 10, 5, 0 dB) — multi-condition training.

Each noisy test condition is repeated with 5 different noise realisations and the mean accuracy is reported. (Simplification: noise is added after segmentation, so this experiment measures the classifier, not the voice-activity detector.)

In [24]:
def add_white_noise(w, snr_db, rng):
    p_signal = np.mean(w ** 2)
    return w + rng.standard_normal(len(w)) * math.sqrt(p_signal / 10 ** (snr_db / 10))

SNRS = [None, 30, 20, 10, 5, 0, -5]                       # None = clean
N_REP = 5
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
test_raw = [word_signals[i] for i in test_idx]
train_raw = [word_signals[i] for i in train_idx]

# noisy test sets (identical for both training conditions)
test_sets = {snr: [np.vstack([word_features(add_white_noise(w, snr, rng) if snr is not None else w) for w in test_raw])
                   for _ in range(1 if snr is None else N_REP)] for snr in SNRS}

# noise-augmented training set
aug_X, aug_y = [X_tr], [y_tr]
for snr in (20, 10, 5, 0):
    aug_X.append(np.vstack([word_features(add_white_noise(w, snr, rng)) for w in train_raw])); aug_y.append(y_tr)
aug_X, aug_y = np.vstack(aug_X), np.concatenate(aug_y)

aug_models = {n: model_zoo()[n][0].set_params(**best_params[n]).fit(aug_X, aug_y) for n in ZOO}

def noise_table(models):
    return pd.DataFrame({("clean" if s is None else f"{s} dB"): {n: 100 * np.mean([accuracy_score(y_te, m.predict(Xt)) for Xt in test_sets[s]])
                                                                  for n, m in models.items()} for s in SNRS})
noise_clean, noise_aug = noise_table(tuned), noise_table(aug_models)

def worst_case(tbl, snr): return tbl[snr].min(), tbl[snr].idxmin(), tbl[snr].max(), tbl[snr].idxmax()

    f"* *Noise-augmented:* at 10 dB the range is {a10[0]:.1f}–{a10[2]:.1f} %, at 0 dB {a0[0]:.1f}–{a0[2]:.1f} %, at −5 dB {am5[0]:.1f}–{am5[2]:.1f} %.  \n"
    f"* Mean accuracy over all models and all noisy conditions (SNR ≤ 10 dB): clean-trained {noise_clean[['10 dB','5 dB','0 dB','-5 dB']].values.mean():.1f} % → "

What the numbers say.

  • Clean-trained: at 10 dB SNR the accuracy ranges from 50.0 % (SVM (RBF)) to 97.4 % (Gaussian NB); at 0 dB from 50.0 % (SVM (RBF)) to 69.4 % (Gaussian NB).
  • Noise-augmented: at 10 dB the range is 99.2–99.9 %, at 0 dB 65.8–95.0 %, at −5 dB 55.7–81.4 %.
  • Mean accuracy over all models and all noisy conditions (SNR ≤ 10 dB): clean-trained 60.8 % → noise-augmented 89.1 %.
  • Augmentation improved 25 of 36 noisy model/SNR cells by more than 0.5 points and made 2 cell(s) worse: Gaussian NB at 5 dB, Gaussian NB at 0 dB.

Lesson. A classifier that is perfect on clean studio-like audio can degrade quickly when the acoustic conditions change, and the models differ in how they fail. Training on data that resemble the deployment conditions (here: noise augmentation) is the first and cheapest remedy. In a real telephone system one would also use a noise-robust front-end (e.g. spectral subtraction, cepstral mean normalisation) and train on real channel noise rather than white noise.

9.3 An end-to-end “telephone operator”¶

Finally we assemble the complete system described in the introduction. Input: a raw recording. Output: the recognised sequence of answers. The system must also fail gracefully when the recording cannot be segmented.

Model choice. Several models tie at the top of the nested cross-validation. We pick the best mean CV accuracy and, among ties, the simplest model (Occam’s razor: fewest assumptions, fastest, easiest to interpret).

In [27]:
SIMPLICITY = ["Logistic Regression", "Gaussian NB", "k-NN", "SVM (RBF)", "Random Forest", "Neural Network (MLP)"]
top_acc = max(np.mean(fold_acc[n]) for n in names)
primary = min([n for n in names if np.isclose(np.mean(fold_acc[n]), top_acc)], key=SIMPLICITY.index)
display(Markdown(f"**Selected model for the demo:** `{primary}` (mean nested-CV accuracy {100*top_acc:.2f} %)."))

def recognise_recording(x, model):
    """Raw recording -> list of 'YES'/'NO' (or None if the recording cannot be segmented into 8 words)."""
    r = segment_words(x)
    if not r["ok"]:
        return None, r
    feats = np.vstack([word_features(x[a:b]) for a, b in r["segments"]])
    return [CLASSES[i] for i in model.predict(feats)], r

def classify_answer(word_wave, model):
    """One spoken answer -> (decision, confidence)."""
    f = word_features(word_wave)[None, :]
    p = model.predict_proba(f)[0, 1] if hasattr(model, "predict_proba") else 1 / (1 + np.exp(-model.decision_function(f)[0]))
    return ("YES", p) if p >= 0.5 else ("NO", 1 - p)

test_files = list(dict.fromkeys(words.loc[test_idx, "file"]))
eval_rows, demo_out = [], {}
for n in names:
    exact, word_ok, total = 0, 0, 0
    for fn in test_files:
        x_f, labs = recordings[fn]
        out, _ = recognise_recording(x_f, tuned[n]); truth = [CLASSES[l] for l in labs]
        exact += out == truth; word_ok += sum(a == b for a, b in zip(out, truth)); total += 8
        if n == primary: demo_out[fn] = (truth, out)
    eval_rows.append({"Model": n, "Recordings fully correct": f"{exact} / {len(test_files)}", "Word accuracy": f"{100*word_ok/total:.2f} %"})
display(Markdown("**Table 11 — End-to-end evaluation on the unseen test recordings (raw audio in, 8-word sequence out)**"))
display(pd.DataFrame(eval_rows).set_index("Model"))

# integration test: the end-to-end path must reproduce the batch predictions of Section 8 exactly
flat = [CLASSES.index(w) for fn in test_files for w in demo_out[fn][1]]
assert flat == list(pred_te[primary]), "end-to-end predictions differ from batch predictions"
print("Integration test passed: end-to-end predictions == batch predictions for", primary)

10. Error analysis¶

A score of 100 % hides information, so we look at (i) every word that was misclassified in the nested cross-validation and (ii) the confidence margin of the selected model: how far the correct words are from the decision boundary. Words close to the boundary are the ones most likely to fail on new data.

1. **The task is easy for every model.** {n_perfect} of {len(names)} models classify all {len(y_te)} unseen test words correctly and the lowest test accuracy is {100*res_te['Accuracy'].min():.2f} %. 11. Discussion and limitations¶

Findings

  1. The task is easy for every model. 6 of 6 models classify all 144 unseen test words correctly and the lowest test accuracy is 100.00 %. The reasons are visible in Figure 5: two acoustically different words, one speaker, a clean recording and informative MFCC statistics make the classes almost linearly separable.
  2. Model choice hardly matters here. Differences of one word (0.69 points on the test set) are well inside the confidence intervals of Table 6, and the tuning grids are flat (Table 5: for every model several settings tie at the best cross-validation score). We therefore select the simplest top model (Logistic Regression), not the one with the highest raw number.
  3. Features matter more than classifiers. Mean accuracy over the three fixed models: majority class 52.7 %, duration only 63.3 %, 13 mean MFCCs 100.0 %, full 52-D set 99.9 % (Table 8).
  4. Preprocessing decides correctness. A one-position shift of the labels caused by a wrong segmentation would corrupt the training data without any error message; the quality-control table and the visual checks are therefore part of the solution, not decoration.
  5. Robustness is the real difference between systems. Accuracy under noise (Figure 8) separates the models far more than clean accuracy does. Noise augmentation raises the mean accuracy over the noisy conditions from 60.8 % to 89.1 %, although not for every model and SNR (see Section 9.2).

Limitations — what these results do not show

  • One speaker, one language, one session. The system recognises the Hebrew words ken/lo from a single male voice. The results say nothing about new speakers, accents, or other languages; a speaker-independent claim would require a multi-speaker corpus such as Google Speech Commands (Warden, 2018).
  • Small data. 472 words from 59 recordings; the test set has 144 words.
  • Segmentation assumes exactly 8 words per recording and relatively clean silence between them; a real telephone system needs a robust endpoint detector that works without knowing the number of words.
  • Noise was added after segmentation and was white; real telephone noise is coloured, non-stationary and also disturbs the voice-activity detector.
  • The comparison is at the ceiling, so “best model” statements are not statistically supported.

Possible extensions: MFCC statistics → sequence models (HMM-GMM, DTW) that keep the temporal order inside the word; CNN on log-Mel spectrograms; speaker-independent evaluation on Speech Commands; real-noise augmentation; confidence-based rejection (“please repeat”) using the margin of Table 14.

**What we did.** We turned 59 usable recordings of the YesNo corpus into **472 labelled words** (one recording with only seven audible words was excluded, not guessed), implemented an MFCC + Δ front-end from scratch (with unit tests), and compared **six classifiers** — including the required SVM and neural network — with a leak-free protocol: recording-grouped hold-out test, tuning on the training data only, and nested 5-fold cross-validation.

**Results.**
* On {len(y_te)} unseen test words the models reach {100*res_te['Accuracy'].min():.2f}–{100*res_te['Accuracy'].max():.2f} % accuracy; the selected model (`{primary}`) makes {int(sel['Errors'])} error(s) (precision {sel['Precision']:.3f}, recall {sel['Recall']:.3f}, F1 {sel['F1']:.3f}, ROC-AUC {sel['ROC-AUC']:.3f}).
* Nested cross-validation over all words gives {', '.join(f"{n} {100*np.mean(fold_acc[n]):.2f} %" for n in names)}.
* Spectral features carry the information (baselines {abl_base:.1f} % and {abl_dur:.1f} % vs. {abl_full:.1f} % for the full feature set); standardisation, standard deviations and Δ-coefficients made no measurable difference on this clean data.
* Under additive white noise the clean-trained models collapse ({int((noise_clean['10 dB'] <= 55).sum())} of {len(noise_clean)} are at chance level at 10 dB SNR), whereas noise-augmented training keeps every model above {noise_aug['5 dB'].min():.0f} % at 5 dB.
* The end-to-end “telephone operator” recognises complete 8-word answers directly from raw audio and rejects recordings it cannot segment.

**Practical value.** The exercise delivers a template for any small speech-classification problem: *(1) look at the data, (2) make sure the labels are aligned, (3) extract compact perceptual features, (4) split by the right unit, (5) tune without touching the test set, (6) report uncertainty, and (7) test the conditions you will face in deployment.* Because every model scores near 100 % on clean single-speaker data, the lasting lessons are about **method** — correct segmentation, leak-free evaluation and robustness testing — rather than about which classifier wins.
"""))

12. Conclusion¶

What we did. We turned 59 usable recordings of the YesNo corpus into 472 labelled words (one recording with only seven audible words was excluded, not guessed), implemented an MFCC + Δ front-end from scratch (with unit tests), and compared six classifiers — including the required SVM and neural network — with a leak-free protocol: recording-grouped hold-out test, tuning on the training data only, and nested 5-fold cross-validation.

Results.

  • On 144 unseen test words the models reach 100.00–100.00 % accuracy; the selected model (Logistic Regression) makes 0 error(s) (precision 1.000, recall 1.000, F1 1.000, ROC-AUC 1.000).
  • Nested cross-validation over all words gives SVM (RBF) 100.00 %, Neural Network (MLP) 100.00 %, k-NN 99.79 %, Logistic Regression 100.00 %, Random Forest 100.00 %, Gaussian NB 100.00 %.
  • Spectral features carry the information (baselines 52.7 % and 63.3 % vs. 99.9 % for the full feature set); standardisation, standard deviations and Δ-coefficients made no measurable difference on this clean data.
  • Under additive white noise the clean-trained models collapse (3 of 6 are at chance level at 10 dB SNR), whereas noise-augmented training keeps every model above 86 % at 5 dB.
  • The end-to-end “telephone operator” recognises complete 8-word answers directly from raw audio and rejects recordings it cannot segment.

Practical value. The exercise delivers a template for any small speech-classification problem: (1) look at the data, (2) make sure the labels are aligned, (3) extract compact perceptual features, (4) split by the right unit, (5) tune without touching the test set, (6) report uncertainty, and (7) test the conditions you will face in deployment. Because every model scores near 100 % on clean single-speaker data, the lasting lessons are about method — correct segmentation, leak-free evaluation and robustness testing — rather than about which classifier wins.

13. Check your understanding¶

Q1. Why do we split the data by recording and not by individual word?

Words of the same recording share microphone, room and speaker state. If some of them are in the training set and others in the test set, the model can exploit recording-specific cues and the test accuracy becomes too optimistic (data leakage).

Q2. What happens to the labels if the segmentation misses one word in a recording?

All following words are paired with the wrong label (a shift by one position), so up to half the words of that recording are mislabelled — silently. That is why we count the bursts, check the durations, and plot the result.

Q3. Why use the Mel scale and a logarithm in MFCC extraction?

The Mel scale mimics the ear’s finer frequency resolution at low frequencies and coarser resolution at high frequencies; the logarithm mimics its roughly logarithmic loudness perception and turns multiplicative effects (vocal tract × source) into additive ones, which the DCT can then separate.

Q4. The test accuracy is 100 %. Can we say the true accuracy is 100 %?

No. With n test words and zero errors, the 95 % Wilson interval is [≈ 97.4 %, 100 %] for n = 144. A finite test set can only bound the true error rate.

Q5. Why must the StandardScaler be inside the cross-validation pipeline?

Fitting it on all data would let information about the test folds (their mean and variance) influence the training — a subtle form of leakage. Inside a pipeline it is fitted on the training folds only.

Q6. Name two reasons why these results cannot be generalised to a real call-centre system.

Single speaker and language; clean recordings; the segmentation assumes exactly 8 words; the noise test is simplified (white noise after segmentation). See Section 11.

Try it yourself¶

  1. Change the frame length to 20 ms / 30 ms and the number of Mel filters to 20 / 40. How do the cross-validation results of Table 8 change?
  2. Add Δ² (acceleration) coefficients to the feature vector. Does the ablation table improve?
  3. Replace the mean/std pooling by a time-normalised representation (resample each MFCC track to 10 frames and flatten). Which classifiers benefit?
  4. Evaluate leave-one-recording-out cross-validation instead of 5-fold and compare the variance of the estimates.
  5. Download the yes and no folders of Google Speech Commands and test the trained model on them. What happens, and why?

Appendix¶

A. How to run¶

Open the notebook in Jupyter or Google Colab and choose Run all. The dataset is downloaded automatically (or set YESNO_DIR to a local copy of waves_yesno). Typical run time: 1–2 minutes on a laptop CPU.
